title: Uranium, Half a Billion Dollars, and a Wall of Indian Flags: What Actually Happened When Modi Landed in Melbourne
excerpt: Australia struck a historic uranium export deal, its largest pension fund committed $347 million to India, and far-right protesters outside Marvel Stadium were outnumbered a thousand to one. For a million Indian Australians, the message was hard to miss.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Australia and India finalized a historic uranium export deal during Modi's visit.
  • AustralianSuper committed $347 million to India's infrastructure fund, signaling investment confidence.
  • Thousands of Indian Australians celebrated Modi's visit, overshadowing a small group of protesters.
  • The Indian diaspora in Australia is the largest overseas-born population, influencing bilateral relations.
  • Modi's tour emphasizes economic partnerships and diaspora diplomacy across the Indo-Pacific.
Historic Uranium Deal
›Australia to export uranium for India's civilian nuclear energy.
›India aims for 100 gigawatts of nuclear capacity by 2047.
›New agreement includes safeguards for peaceful use.
›Australia seeks to reduce trade dependence on China.
Australia and India struck a historic uranium export deal on Thursday in Melbourne, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrapped up the centrepiece of his three-nation Indo-Pacific tour with a CEO forum, a landmark energy agreement, and a stadium reception that drew thousands of Indian Australians — and a handful of determined opponents. The uranium arrangement, finalised during bilateral talks between Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, commits Australia to exporting uranium for India's civilian nuclear energy programme. India has targeted 100 gigawatts of nuclear capacity by 2047 and has long coveted Australia's reserves — the world's largest — while Canberra wants to reduce its trade dependence on China. "Australia and India are close partners and even closer friends," Albanese told reporters after the signing. "The arrangement facilitates Australian uranium exports to India to help increase the share of non-fossil fuel power capacity." A nuclear cooperation pact between the two countries has existed since 2014, but actual exports remained minimal over fears the material could be diverted to India's weapons programme. The new agreement locks in safeguards ensuring nuclear fuel is used exclusively for peaceful purposes. ## Half a Billion Dollars in a Single Announcement The energy deal was not the only headline. AustralianSuper, Australia's largest pension fund with more than A$400 billion in assets under management, announced it would invest a further A$500 million (roughly $347 million) in India's National Investment and Infrastructure Fund. For a diaspora community that has spent decades arguing India is a reliable destination for long-term capital, the commitment was a validation in hard currency. > **"Albanese, evidently impressed, called Modi a "living bridge" between Australia and India — language that has historically been used to describe the diaspora itself."** Modi used the India-Australia CEO Forum to make his pitch directly. "India provides a safe, stable and sustainable growth option for your funds," he told the room of business leaders, urging investment in India's road, port, rail, and urban infrastructure. He also floated cooperation on low-carbon aluminium projects, signalling an expansion of the two countries' energy partnership beyond uranium and renewables. Albanese, evidently impressed, called Modi a "living bridge" between Australia and India — language that has historically been used to describe the diaspora itself. ![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg) ## Outside Marvel Stadium, Two Australias The warmth inside Melbourne's corporate conference rooms collided with something uglier outside Marvel Stadium, where Modi was scheduled to address the diaspora on Thursday evening.
Investment Confidence Soars
›AustralianSuper invests A$500 million in India's infrastructure fund.
›Total assets under management: A$400 billion.
›Investment reflects confidence in India's long-term capital potential.
›Modi promotes India as a stable growth option for investors.
A group of roughly two dozen far-right protesters gathered outside the arena, shouting anti-immigration slogans and holding banners demanding the expulsion of Indians from Australia. They were comprehensively outnumbered — by thousands of people waving Indian tricolours, banging drums, and queuing for entry in Melbourne's winter chill. Police maintained a heavy presence. The confrontation, such as it was, lasted longer in social media clips than it did on the ground. The scene encapsulated a tension that Indian Australians have navigated with increasing frequency. Around one million people in Australia claim Indian ancestry — making them the country's largest overseas-born population. That visibility has brought both political clout and backlash. ## The Diaspora's Growing Weight Modi's three-nation tour — Indonesia, then Australia, then New Zealand — has been an exercise in diaspora diplomacy. In Jakarta he signed defence deals worth ₹5,500 crore, including the BrahMos cruise missile system. In Melbourne, the deliverables were economic and symbolic: the uranium deal, the AustralianSuper investment, and the "living bridge" framing that positions the Indian community not as a lobbying group but as a structural pillar of the bilateral relationship.
The Indian Australian Community
›1 million Indian Australians, the largest overseas-born group.
›Protesters outside Marvel Stadium were outnumbered a thousand to one.
›Modi's visit highlights the community's political clout.
›Tensions between visibility and backlash are increasing.
For the million-strong Indian Australian community, the takeaway was straightforward: when their prime minister visits, deals get signed, capital moves, and the host country's leader reaches for the most generous metaphors available. The far-right protesters outside the stadium made it equally clear that not everyone is celebrating. Modi departs Melbourne on Friday for Auckland, where he will become the first Indian Prime Minister to visit New Zealand in four decades. Three hundred and fifty thousand Indian New Zealanders are expected to greet him — and, if Melbourne is any guide, a few will be there to object.

The uranium deal and AustralianSuper investment validate the community's decades-long argument that India is a reliable destination for Australian capital — while the far-right protest outside Marvel Stadium underscores the backlash their visibility now attracts.
